Blank completion, contrast clue (including received view then finding)
Blank completion, cause or consequence clue

items.passage: Historian Pekka Hämäläinen’s The Comanche Empire (2008) is ______ scholarship that portrays the Indigenous peoples of the American Southwest predominantly as victims of European colonization: in Hämäläinen’s account, the Comanches were a formidable imperial power for over a century, combining raiding with profitable commerce and extracting costly gifts from Spanish officials as the price of peace.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “A corrective to” means something that sets right an earlier error or imbalance. The text says that other scholarship portrays the Indigenous peoples of the Southwest mainly as victims of colonization, whereas Hämäläinen presents the Comanches as a formidable imperial power for over a century, one that even extracted gifts from Spanish officials. His book therefore corrects the one-sided picture that scholarship gives.

A.why_wrong: “A vindication of” would mean the book shows that scholarship to be right. Instead it presents the Comanches as a dominant power rather than as victims, which challenges that scholarship.

B.why_wrong: “A pastiche of” means a work that imitates the style of other works. Nothing suggests the book imitates earlier scholarship; it offers a different account of Indigenous peoples.

D.why_wrong: “A recapitulation of” means a summary or restatement. The book does not restate the scholarship that portrays Indigenous peoples as victims; it argues against that picture.

sources.what: La Vie des Idées review of Hämäläinen, The Comanche Empire (Yale, 2008): the book reverses the perspective that reduced Native peoples to the role of victims, presenting a Comanche native empire that dominated the Southwest

band7_moves: option-set rarity: all four options past rank 20,000 (vindication 20,373; corrective 37,103; recapitulation 55,815; pastiche absent)
the clue is a contrast of two portrayals, a level more abstract than the key, so the student must infer the relation (correction) rather than match a synonym
items.notes: Subject: history (historiography of the Comanche). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (histories cast Native peoples as victims; the book shows an imperial power; so it corrects them). One reversal, one unsupported, one wrong-relation option; no near synonym of corrective is offered, because rebuttal, refutation or riposte would all fit. Every detail is in the review: raiding went hand in hand with profitable commerce, peace with the Comanches was paid for with costly gifts from New Spain, and they were a genuine power for over a century. The book's dates (1706 to 1874) are left out. Raw freq.txt ranks given above; band-7 check 1 passes (4 of 4 past 10,000), check 2 passes (pastiche unseen).

band7.why: B6 with a transferred noun sense (a corrective to) reached by inferring a relation from two contrasting portrayals; every option past 20,000 raw and 3 of 4 past 10,000 corrected (corrective 5,680), rarest distractor unseen (pastiche): checks 1 to 3 pass and it is not the band-5 pattern. Rarity carries it; no near-synonym distractor, because rebuttal, refutation and antidote would each fit, and forcing one would add a second answer.

items.passage: For decades the Metropolitan Museum of Art exhibited three terracotta warriors as genuine ancient Etruscan sculptures. In 1960, however, chemical tests showed that the statues’ glaze was ______: it contained manganese, an ingredient that Etruscan potters had never used. Soon afterward, sculptor Alfredo Fioravanti confessed that he had helped make the figures decades earlier.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Anachronistic” means belonging to a different time from the one something comes from or claims to come from. The text says the glaze contained manganese, an ingredient Etruscan potters never used, so the glaze could not belong to the ancient period the statues supposedly came from, and a sculptor later confessed to helping make them.

B.why_wrong: “Archaic” means very old or belonging to an earlier time. The tests showed the reverse problem: the glaze contained an ingredient the Etruscans never used, so it was too recent for an ancient work, not too old.

C.why_wrong: “Variegated” means marked with patches of different colors. The text says nothing about the colors of the glaze; the tests concerned what it contained.

D.why_wrong: “Friable” means easily crumbled. The text gives no information about whether the glaze crumbles; the tests concerned an ingredient that showed the glaze did not date from Etruscan times.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Etruscan terracotta warriors: bought by the Met 1915 to 1921; in 1960 chemical tests of the statue glazes showed the presence of manganese, an ingredient that Etruscans had never used; Alfredo Fioravanti signed a confession on January 5, 1961; the Met announced the forgeries on February 15, 1961

band7_moves: option-set rarity: all four options past rank 20,000 on both the raw and corrected measures (archaic 23,550; variegated 24,242; friable 71,307; anachronistic unseen)
near-synonym distractor from the key's field that fails on one feature (archaic: old, not out of its time)
clue phrased in a different register from the key (an ingredient the Etruscans had never used)
items.notes: Subject: humanities (art history, forgery). Key letter A. Steps: 2 (an ingredient the Etruscans never used means the glaze cannot belong to Etruscan times, so it is out of its time). Apocryphal and inauthentic were rejected as distractors because a forged glaze is loosely inauthentic. Reviewer replaced iridescent and soluble (corrected ranks 6,509 and 7,650, so the rare key sat beside two common distractors, the band-5 pattern) with variegated and friable. Vitreous and lustrous were not used: every glaze is glassy and lustrous, so either could be defended loosely.

band7.why: B1 with a rare key (anachronistic, unseen in freq.txt) reached by a two-step inference (never used by Etruscans, so out of its time), a near-synonym trap (archaic: old, not out of its time) and, after the fix, two rare unsupported words (variegated 24k, friable 71k): checks 1 to 4 pass on raw and corrected ranks. Before the fix it read band 5 to 6 (two common distractors a student could drop at once).

fixes: replaced distractors iridescent and soluble with variegated and friable: on the corrected measure iridescent (6,509) and soluble (7,650) were under 10,000 with the key the rarest option, the band-5 guard pattern; all four options now past 20,000

items.passage: Because Greenland’s Norse settlers vanished about five centuries ago, they have often been characterized as ______ colonists. Yet a team of researchers analyzing isotopes in eighty Norse skeletons found that the settlers ate progressively more seal over time: by the fourteenth century, seals made up 50 to 80 percent of their diet.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Hidebound” means rigidly attached to old ways and unwilling to change. The word “Yet” signals that the researchers’ finding contradicts the usual portrayal of the settlers. The finding is that they shifted their diet toward seals over time, which shows they adapted, so the usual characterization must have been of colonists who would not change.

A.why_wrong: “Resourceful” describes what the finding shows, settlers who adapted by eating more seal. Because “Yet” introduces a finding that contradicts the usual portrayal, that characterization cannot have been of resourceful colonists.

B.why_wrong: “Itinerant” means traveling from place to place. A finding about what the settlers ate does nothing to contradict a portrayal of them as wanderers, so the contrast signaled by “Yet” would make no sense.

C.why_wrong: “Bellicose” means eager to fight. A finding that the settlers ate more seal over time says nothing about how warlike they were, so it could not challenge such a portrayal.

sources.what: ScienceNordic 2012, Greenland's Viking settlers feasted on seals, then left: isotopic analysis of 80 Norse skeletons shows the settlers ate gradually more seals; by the 14th century seals made up 50 to 80 percent of their diet; challenges the prevailing view of the Norse as farmers who stubbornly stuck to agriculture and the theory of an inability to adapt; settlers disappeared some 500 years ago

band7_moves: option-set rarity: all four options past rank 20,000 (resourceful 24,584; itinerant 28,473; bellicose 52,632; hidebound 66,900)
blank on the received view, with the finding's trait (resourceful) offered as the reversal
direction left implicit: the view is never restated, only contradicted by the finding
items.notes: Subject: social science (archaeology). Key letter D. Steps: 2 (Yet means the finding contradicts the view; the finding shows adaptation; so the view was of inflexible farmers). Credited to a team of researchers, as the source names a collaboration (Aarhus, Copenhagen, National Museum of Denmark, Simon Fraser) rather than a single lead author. The noun is colonists, not farmers, so that the Yet clause can contradict only the adjective (farmers against seal-eaters would be a second contrast). Fastidious, ascetic and improvident were rejected as distractors because each could be read loosely as contradicted by a change of diet. Not the walrus-ivory (inferences w2b3_18) or L'Anse aux Meadows subjects.

band7.why: B3 with the blank on the received view, direction left implicit (Yet plus a finding of adaptation), the finding's trait (resourceful) as the reversal, and all four options past 20,000 on both measures (bellicose 52,632; hidebound 66,900): checks 1 to 3 pass. No near-synonym distractor; fastidious, ascetic and improvident could each be read as contradicted by a change of diet.

items.passage: The notion that the blackpoll warbler, a songbird weighing roughly 12 grams, migrates nonstop across the Atlantic Ocean each autumn is no longer ______. Using miniature geolocators that record light levels, William DeLuca and colleagues tracked blackpolls and determined that the birds traveled 2,270 to 2,770 kilometers over open water in up to three days.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Unproven” means not yet shown to be true. The phrase “no longer” signals a change, and the next sentence explains it: DeLuca’s tracking data showed that blackpolls really do make the long flight over open water. The idea, which had lacked direct evidence, has now been demonstrated.

A.why_wrong: “Attested” means supported by evidence. The tracking data are new evidence for the idea, so saying the idea is no longer attested reverses what the text describes.

C.why_wrong: “Grueling” means exhausting. The tracking data show that the crossing happens; nothing in the text suggests that the crossing, or the idea of it, has become less exhausting.

D.why_wrong: “Circuitous” means roundabout. The text describes a direct flight over open water, and nothing suggests that the idea, or the route, was once thought to be roundabout.

sources.what: Smithsonian repository record of DeLuca et al. 2015, Transoceanic migration by a 12 g songbird, Biology Letters: first irrefutable evidence from light-level geolocators that blackpoll warblers fly nonstop over the Atlantic, 2,270 to 2,770 km, up to 3 days; the flight had been suspected for decades

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ornithology). Key letter B. Steps: 2 (no longer X plus new direct evidence, so X must be the state before the evidence: unproven). Negated frame stated plainly, band 6 as the plan asks; one negation-flip reversal (attested). Anecdotal, rumored and hypothetical were not used: the first two fit loosely, and hypothetical shares a stem with official options (hypothesis, hypothesized). Raw freq.txt ranks: attested 22,718; unproven 69,099; grueling 25,148 (reviewer replaced perilous, 6,611, two bands below the rest); circuitous 25,307.

band7.why: B5 with the negation stated plainly (no longer) and a negation-flip reversal (attested), the band-6 recipe; two steps (no longer X plus new direct evidence, so X was unproven). All four options past 20,000 after the fix, so a strong band 6; the plain frame keeps it from 7, as the plan intends.

fixes: replaced distractor perilous (rank 6,611) with grueling (25,148) so all four options sit past 20,000, one frequency band
source URL (repository.si.edu) returns 403 to the fetcher; core claim confirmed by search (DeLuca et al. 2015, Biology Letters 11: first direct evidence, 2,270 to 2,770 km, up to 3 days)

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Kareem Haggag and Giovanni Paci found that when the payment screens in New York City taxis displayed higher suggested tips, passengers generally tipped more. Because the elevated suggestions also prompted a larger proportion of passengers to forgo leaving any tip on their credit cards, however, the higher defaults represented only a ______ success for drivers.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: A “qualified” success is a limited one, a success with reservations. The text says the higher suggestions raised tips but also led more passengers to leave no card tip at all, so the gain for drivers came with a real drawback.

A.why_wrong: “Resounding” means complete and emphatic. The text points to a drawback, more passengers leaving no tip, and “only” signals a limited success, not a complete one.

B.why_wrong: “Transient” means lasting only a short time. The drawback in the text is that some passengers skipped the tip, not that the higher tips faded over time.

D.why_wrong: “Clandestine” means secret. Nothing in the text suggests that the higher tips were hidden from anyone; the text describes a drawback that limited the success.

sources.what: IDEAS/RePEc abstract of Haggag and Paci, Default Tips, AEJ: Applied 2014: using 13 million NYC taxi rides, default tip suggestions have a large impact on tip amounts; a higher proportion of customers opt to leave no credit card tip when presented with the higher suggested amounts

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics). Key letter C. Steps: 2 (higher tips on average, but more riders leaving none, so the success was limited). Key in a secondary sense (qualified = limited), the usual SAT sense test. Partial, modest and mixed were not offered (each would also fit; modest is an official key). Simplified: the exact menus (15/20/25 against 20/25/30 percent) and the fare threshold are left out. Raw freq.txt ranks: resounding 16,154; transient 12,088 (reviewer replaced temporary, 4,540, two bands below the rest); qualified 11,004; clandestine 19,285.

band7.why: B2 with the cause in a Because clause and the key in a secondary sense (qualified = limited), two steps; each distractor is ruled out by one stated fact (only, no time, no secrecy) and the option set sits at 10,000 to 20,000, so a solid band 6, not 7.

fixes: replaced distractor temporary (rank 4,540) with transient (12,088) so all four options sit in the 10,000 to 20,000 band; ephemeral was rejected because it breaks the article (a ______ success)

items.passage: Hair ice, silky filaments that emerge from decaying branches on humid winter nights, is not a purely ______ phenomenon. Diana Hofmann and colleagues detected the fungus Exidiopsis effusa on every hair-ice-producing specimen they examined, and treating the wood with heat or fungicide prevented the filaments from developing.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Abiotic” means not involving living things. The text says a fungus was present on every piece of wood that produced hair ice and that heat or fungicide, which kill or block the fungus, stopped the ice from forming. Hair ice therefore depends on a living organism and is not simply a result of nonliving physical processes.

B.why_wrong: “Optical” means relating to light or sight. The findings about the fungus explain how hair ice forms, not how it looks or how light passes through it.

C.why_wrong: “Transitory” means short-lived. The findings concern what hair ice needs in order to form, not how long it lasts.

D.why_wrong: “Cyclical” means occurring in repeated cycles. The text says nothing about hair ice recurring in a pattern; it explains that a fungus is needed for the ice to form.

sources.what: Hofmann, Preuss and Mätzler 2015, Evidence for biological shaping of hair ice, Biogeosciences 12: one species, Exidiopsis effusa, was present on all investigated samples; treatment by heat and fungicide suppresses the formation of hair ice; the fungus shapes the ice hairs

items.notes: Subject: natural science (mycology, ice physics). Key letter A. Negation in the frame (not purely), clue in the next sentence. Microbial, atmospheric, random and coincidental were rejected as distractors because each also makes a defensible sentence (hair ice is not purely microbial either, and the fungus result shows it is not random). Raw freq.txt ranks: abiotic unseen (modern biology term), optical 26,279, transitory 21,119, cyclical unseen.

items.passage: Marathon runners appear to be ______ round numbers: analyzing millions of race results, Eric Allen and colleagues discovered substantial clustering of finishing times just below thresholds such as four hours and determined that runners in danger of narrowly missing such a target accelerate near the finish.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Spurred on by” means urged to greater effort by. The text says finishing times cluster just below round thresholds such as four hours and that runners about to miss such a target speed up near the finish, so round numbers push runners to try harder.

A.why_wrong: “Oblivious to” means unaware of. Runners who speed up to beat a round time are clearly aware of it.

B.why_wrong: “Daunted by” means discouraged by. The runners in the text respond to a round time by speeding up, not by losing heart.

C.why_wrong: “Embarrassed by” means made to feel awkward or ashamed by. The text says nothing about how runners feel about round numbers, only that they speed up to finish under them.

sources.what: NBER working paper w20343 (Allen, Dechow, Pope, Wu), Reference-Dependent Preferences: Evidence from Marathon Runners: 9.5 million finishing times; round numbers such as a four-hour marathon act as reference points, producing bunching just below them, driven by planning and adjustments in effort near the finish line

items.notes: Subject: social science (behavioral economics). Key letter D. Distractor mix: one reversal, one wrong-direction near miss (discouraged rather than spurred), one unsupported. Raw freq.txt ranks: oblivious 9,178; daunted 15,061; embarrassed 4,505; spurred 9,922.

items.passage: Spawning salmon ______ the forests bordering Alaskan streams. James Helfield and Robert Naiman determined that streamside vegetation derives nearly a quarter of its foliar nitrogen from salmon and that Sitka spruce adjacent to spawning sites grew over three times as rapidly as spruce at locations lacking salmon.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Fertilize” means to make soil or plants more productive by adding nutrients. The text says streamside trees and shrubs get nearly a quarter of the nitrogen in their leaves (their foliar nitrogen), a nutrient, from salmon, and that spruce near spawning sites grew more than three times as fast as spruce where there were no salmon.

A.why_wrong: “Deplete” means to use up. The text says salmon supply nitrogen that the trees use and that trees near spawning sites grow faster, the opposite of draining the forests.

C.why_wrong: “Pollinate” means to carry pollen between flowers. Salmon help the trees by supplying nitrogen, not by carrying pollen.

D.why_wrong: “Irrigate” means to supply with water. The text credits salmon with supplying nitrogen, not water, to the trees.

sources.what: Helfield and Naiman 2001, Effects of salmon-derived nitrogen on riparian forest growth, Ecology 82: riparian trees and shrubs near spawning streams derive 22 to 24 percent of their foliar nitrogen from spawning salmon; basal growth of Sitka spruce at spawning sites was more than triple that at reference sites (Chichagof Island, southeast Alaska)

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ecology). Key letter B. Two near misses from the helping-plants field (pollinate, irrigate) and one reversal. How the nitrogen reaches the soil (carcasses carried by bears and other animals) is left out because the source abstract does not state it. Not the Elwha dam removal (TSP w2b2_24) or salmon homing (CTC w2b2_14) subjects. Raw freq.txt ranks: deplete 70,728; fertilize 71,168; pollinate unseen; irrigate unseen.

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: Because eL Seed’s mural Perception extends across approximately fifty separate buildings in Cairo’s Manshiyat Naser neighborhood, its Arabic calligraphy is largely ______: from most vantage points within the district, the painted fragments appear disconnected from one another, and the inscription can be read properly only from a particular spot on nearby Mokattam Mountain.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Illegible” means impossible to read. Because the mural is spread across about fifty separate buildings, its painted fragments appear disconnected from most places in the neighborhood, and the text says the inscription can be read properly only from one spot on Mokattam Mountain.

A.why_wrong: “Weathered” means worn by the weather. The text says nothing about the condition of the paint; the problem it describes is that the fragments come together only from one spot.

B.why_wrong: “Fluorescent” means glowing brightly. The text gives no information about the colors of the paint, only about where the inscription can be read from.

D.why_wrong: “Provisional” means temporary or arranged for the time being. Nothing in the text suggests the mural is meant to be temporary; the text explains why it can be read from only one place.

sources.what: Hyperallergic, March 2016, on eL Seed's Perception: the piece covers 50 buildings in Manshiyat Naser, Cairo; its Arabic calligraphy (a quote by Saint Athanasius of Alexandria) appears fragmented and can be read properly only from a spot on the nearby Mokattam Mountain

items.notes: Subject: humanities (public art, calligraphy). Key letter C. Cause in the Because clause (spread across fifty buildings), consequence in the blank, restated after the colon; every option fits the frame (largely ______), so the clue, not the collocation, decides. Inconspicuous, disorienting and monochrome were rejected as distractors because each could be defended loosely. The year is left out (sources give 2015 or 2016). Raw freq.txt ranks: weathered 1,160; fluorescent unseen; illegible 30,558; provisional 26,070.

items.passage:
The following text is from Gertrude Atherton’s 1908 novel The Gorgeous Isle. Mrs. Nunn has fainted on learning that her niece, Anne, intends to marry, and Anne has been anxiously administering restoratives.

But Mrs. Nunn may have been less time reviving than Anne <u>fancied</u>, for when she finally opened her eyes they were very hard and her features singularly composed.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “fancied” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: In the text, “fancied” means supposed, or believed. When Mrs. Nunn opens her eyes they are hard and her face is already calm and controlled, which suggests she had come to herself some time earlier; she spent less time reviving than Anne believed.

B.why_wrong: “Fancied” can mean desired, as when someone fancies a cup of tea, but Anne is anxiously trying to revive her aunt and would not want the recovery to take longer; the text is about what Anne believed, not what she wanted.

C.why_wrong: “Fancied” can mean favored to win, as when a racehorse is fancied, but nothing in the text involves a contest; the point is that Anne misjudged how long her aunt took to revive.

D.why_wrong: “Fancied” can mean admired or took a liking to, but that sense makes no sense with a length of time; the text is about what Anne thought had happened.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Gertrude Atherton, The Gorgeous Isle: A Romance; Scene: Nevis, B.W.I. 1842 (1908); Anne tells her aunt Mrs. Nunn she will marry Mr. Warner, Mrs. Nunn faints, Anne administers restoratives; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1908, public domain). Key letter A. A common word in a less common sense (fancied = supposed), as in the medium models 2.3 (quality) and 2.19 (assumed). All three distractors are other senses of fancy. Imagined and pictured were not offered because each is a near synonym of the key. The excerpt is the sentence that ends the paragraph; the opening sentence of that paragraph (She fell back limp ...) is summarized in the context line. Reviewer change: the item first tested composed (key Self-possessed), the same sense as batch b8 item 17 (collected, key Calm), so the target was moved to fancied in the same sentence. Raw freq.txt ranks: supposed 342; desired 746; favored 2,497; admired 2,811.

fixes: retargeted from composed (key Self-possessed) to fancied (key Supposed) in the same sentence: b8 item 17 tests collected with key Calm, a near-synonym key; new options, explanation and distractors

items.passage: Two-year-olds can ______ new words simply by overhearing them. In a study by psychologist Nameera Akhtar and colleagues, toddlers who heard an adult use an invented word while conversing with another person learned it about as well as toddlers whom the adult addressed directly.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Absorb” means to take in and learn. The text says toddlers who only overheard an invented word learned it about as well as toddlers who were spoken to directly.

A.why_wrong: “Resist” means to refuse to accept. The toddlers in the study learned the overheard words, so they did not resist them.

B.why_wrong: “Mispronounce” means to say incorrectly. The study tested whether toddlers learned the words, and nothing in the text suggests they said them wrongly.

C.why_wrong: “Recite” means to repeat aloud from memory. The text says the toddlers learned the words, not that they repeated them aloud.

sources.what: Akhtar, Jipson and Callanan 2001, Learning Words through Overhearing, Child Development 72: 2-year-olds learned novel words used by others in overheard conversation and performed about as well when overhearing as when addressed directly

items.notes: Subject: social science (developmental psychology). Key letter D. Restatement in the next sentence. Credited to the lead author, Nameera Akhtar. Acquire and learn were not used as the key: acquire is an official option and learn appears in the passage. Raw freq.txt ranks: resist 3,187; mispronounce unseen; recite 18,405; absorb 13,402.

items.passage: Footage recorded in 2016 off Western Australia, the first of a living ruby seadragon, suggests that the fish can ______ objects with its tail. Unlike common and leafy seadragons, it appears capable of curling its tail around things and holding on.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Grip” means to take hold of something firmly. The text says the ruby seadragon appears able to curl its tail around things and hold on, which common and leafy seadragons cannot do.

A.why_wrong: “Sting” means to wound with a sharp point. Nothing in the text suggests that the seadragon’s tail can wound anything.

C.why_wrong: “Camouflage” means to hide by blending in. The footage described in the text shows the tail curling around things, not hiding them.

D.why_wrong: “Release” means to let go. The text says the seadragon curls its tail around things and holds on, the opposite of letting go.

sources.what: National Geographic 2017, Rare Ruby Seadragon Caught on Video for First Time: footage from Western Australia's Recherche Archipelago (team of Greg Rouse, Josefin Stiller, Nerida Wilson, April 2016) is the first of the fish alive and suggests the ruby seadragon can use its curled tail to grasp objects; common and leafy seadragons can't grab objects with their tails

items.notes: Subject: natural science (marine biology). Key letter B. No researcher named: the paper's lead author (Stiller) and the team leader (Rouse) differ, so the text credits the footage, not a person. Raw freq.txt ranks: sting 642; grip 3,583; camouflage unseen; release 3,675.

items.passage: Ethiopian-born painter Wosene Worke Kosrof ______ the characters of the Amharic script in his paintings. He stretches, distorts, and rearranges the letters until they no longer spell out readable words and instead become abstract shapes, gestures, and patterns.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Reshapes” means changes the form of something. The text says Wosene stretches, distorts, and rearranges the Amharic letters until they become abstract shapes and patterns rather than readable words.

A.why_wrong: “Erases” means removes. Wosene keeps the characters in his paintings; he changes their form rather than removing them.

B.why_wrong: “Memorizes” means learns by heart. The text describes what Wosene does to the letters on the canvas, not what he learns.

D.why_wrong: “Illuminates” can mean decorates a manuscript with color and gold. The text describes the letters being stretched and rearranged, not decorated.

sources.what: Winfield Gallery artist page: Ethiopian-born painter Wosene Worke Kosrof elongates, distorts, inverts, dissects and recombines the shapes of Amharic script; the script images are divested of literal meanings and become gesture, dance, music, movement

items.notes: Subject: humanities (painting). Key letter C. Restatement in the next sentence. Transforms was not used as the key because transformed is an official option. Raw freq.txt ranks: erases 38,962; memorizes 63,620; reshapes unseen; illuminates 30,559.

items.passage: Lyda Conley ______ Kansas City’s Huron Cemetery, where her mother and other Wyandot people were buried. After Congress authorized selling the land in 1906, she initiated a lawsuit to block the sale, and she and her sister kept a vigil over the graves from a shack.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Safeguarded” means protected. The text says Conley filed a lawsuit to block the sale of the cemetery and, with her sister, kept watch over the graves from a shack.

B.why_wrong: “Auctioned” means sold to the highest bidder. Conley tried to stop the cemetery from being sold; the text says she filed a lawsuit to block the sale.

C.why_wrong: “Excavated” means dug up. Conley wanted the graves left where they were, and nothing in the text suggests she dug at the cemetery.

D.why_wrong: “Photographed” means took pictures of. The text describes Conley’s lawsuit and her watch over the graves, not any photographs.

sources.what: National Women's History Museum biography of Lyda Conley: in 1906 Congress approved selling the Huron Indian Cemetery in Kansas City, Kansas, where her mother and hundreds of Wyandotte were buried; she sued to stop it, argued before the Supreme Court in 1910, and with her sister Helena built a shack (Fort Conley) at the entrance and guarded the graves

items.notes: Subject: history (Native American legal history). Key letter A. Defended and protected were not used as the key because both are existing option words; the passage avoids guard so the key does not echo it. The Supreme Court appearance is left out to keep the passage at the cell's length. Raw freq.txt ranks: safeguarded 14,871; auctioned 11,781; excavated 34,114; photographed 5,890.

fixes: source URL (womenshistory.org) blocks the fetcher; core claim confirmed by search (1906 sale act, Conley suit, Fort Conley shack with her sister)

items.passage:
The following text is from Onoto Watanna’s 1923 novel Cattle.

[Bull Langdon] knew the country well, and had almost as <u>keen</u> a sense of smell as the cattle themselves. He had boasted that he could “sniff his way” anywhere through the foothill country, and that his long years of night riding had given him a cat’s eyes.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “keen” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: In the text, “keen” means sharp, or highly sensitive. Langdon’s sense of smell is almost as good as the cattle’s, and he boasts that he can “sniff his way” anywhere.

A.why_wrong: “Keen” can mean eager, as in being keen to begin, but a sense of smell cannot be eager; the text is describing how well Langdon can smell.

C.why_wrong: “Keen” can describe a bitter, biting wind, but the text is describing how well Langdon can smell, not anything harsh or painful.

D.why_wrong: “Keen on” can mean devoted to something, but the text is describing how sensitive Langdon’s nose is, not what he is devoted to.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Onoto Watanna (Winnifred Eaton), Cattle (1923); Bull Langdon, owner of the Bar Q ranch in Alberta, seeks the trail through the timber at night; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1923, public domain in the US). Key letter B. All three distractors are other senses of keen. Bracketed name replaces the pronoun He, as CB does ([Jay Gatsby] in 2.3). Clever, shrewd and intense were not offered (clever and shrewd are existing option words; intense fits the sentence).

items.passage:
The following text is from Mary Hallock Foote’s 1902 novel The Desert and the Sown. The colonel’s guest has just taken charge of his daughter’s wedding clothes.

The colonel’s papers failed to <u>hold</u> him somehow. He rose and paced the room with his short, stiff-kneed tread. He stopped and stared into the fire; his face began to get red.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “hold” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: In the text, “hold” means engage, or keep someone’s attention. The colonel’s papers fail to keep him interested: he gets up, paces the room, and stares into the fire.

A.why_wrong: “Hold” can mean own, as when someone holds land or shares, but papers cannot own the colonel; the point is that they fail to keep his attention.

B.why_wrong: “Hold” can mean grasp, as when a person holds a cup, but papers cannot physically grip the colonel; the point is that they fail to keep his interest.

C.why_wrong: “Hold” can mean host, as in holding a meeting, which makes no sense for papers and the colonel.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Mary Hallock Foote, The Desert and the Sown (1902), chapter II, Introducing a Son-in-Law; Mrs. Bogardus, visiting, has said she will set her people to work on Moya's wedding clothes; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (novel, 1902, public domain). Key letter D. All three distractors are other senses of hold. Contain and restrain were not offered: contain can mean restrain, and the colonel's rising anger makes that reading defensible. The guest is Mrs. Bogardus, mother of the man Moya will marry; she has just said she will have Moya's wedding clothes made.

items.passage:
The following text is from Octave Thanet’s 1893 short story “An Assisted Providence.” A minister, Mr. Gilling, has asked Harry Lossing whether he really meant to put two large bills in the church collection.

“I intended to put in two bills,” said he. Gilling gave a little gasp—so little, only a quick ear could have <u>caught</u> it; but Harry’s ear is quick.
items.stem: As used in the text, what does the word “caught” most nearly mean?
items.explanation: In the text, “caught” means heard. Gilling’s gasp is so quiet that only a person with a quick ear could have heard it, and Harry’s ear is quick.

B.why_wrong: “Caught” can mean trapped, as when an animal is caught, but a gasp cannot be trapped; the text is about noticing a quiet sound.

C.why_wrong: “Caught” can mean contracted, as when someone catches a cold, but no one catches an illness here; the text is about hearing a small gasp.

D.why_wrong: “Caught” can mean boarded, as in catching a train, which makes no sense for a gasp.

sources.what: Project Gutenberg text of Octave Thanet, Stories of a Western Town (1893), story An Assisted Providence: Harry Lossing has put two bills he took for fives in the collection; the Rev. Mr. Gilling comes to ask whether he meant to give so much; excerpt copied exactly

items.notes: Subject: literature (short story, 1893, public domain). Key letter A. All three distractors are other senses of catch. Typography: the Gutenberg text prints INTENDED in capitals for italics and -- for the dash; rendered here as plain intended and a closed em dash, as CB transcripts drop italics.

items.passage: Guillermo Amico and Marcelo Aizen found that Tristerix corymbosus, a South American mistletoe, is ______ a small marsupial, Dromiciops australis. The animal eats the mistletoe’s seeds and deposits them, ready to sprout, on trees, and in 500 hours of observation, the researchers saw no birds eating the plant’s seeds.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Tied to” means closely connected with or dependent on. The text says the marsupial eats the mistletoe’s seeds and leaves them ready to sprout on trees, and that no birds were seen eating them, so the plant relies on this one animal to spread its seeds.

A.why_wrong: “Foreign to” means unfamiliar to or unconnected with. The text describes the marsupial regularly eating the mistletoe’s seeds and spreading them.

B.why_wrong: “Menaced by” means put in danger by. Although the marsupial eats the mistletoe’s seeds, the text says it deposits them ready to sprout on trees, so the animal helps the plant rather than endangering it.

D.why_wrong: “Shielded from” means protected from. The mistletoe is not kept away from the marsupial; the animal eats its seeds and spreads them.

sources.what: Science News 2001 on Amico and Aizen (Nature 2000, Mistletoe seed dispersal by a marsupial): the nocturnal, squirrel-size Dromiciops australis eats seeds of a South American mistletoe, Tristerix corymbosus, and excretes them onto trees; 98 percent are intact and ready to sprout; in 500 hours of observation no birds ate the mistletoe

items.notes: Subject: natural science (ecology). Key letter C. Dependent on and reliant on were not used as the key: depended on is an official option and reliant on is our own earlier key. The marsupial is named as in the source (D. australis; it is now usually called D. gliroides, the monito del monte). Raw freq.txt ranks: foreign 2,046; menaced 8,784; tied 2,199; shielded 3,909. Closely was dropped from the frame so that every option fits the slot grammatically.

items.passage: The portraits Sanlé Sory made at Volta Photo, the studio he opened in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960, are ______ the youth culture that flourished in Burkina Faso after independence. In them, teenagers and young adults pose as their favorite musicians or model the latest fashions, holding props such as radios, telephones, and lamps.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “A record of” means something that preserves an account of. The text says Sory’s portraits show young people of the time posing as musicians, modeling fashions, and holding props such as radios and telephones, so the photographs capture that youth culture.

A.why_wrong: “A departure from” means a break with. The portraits show young people taking part in the culture of their time, so they are not a break from it.

C.why_wrong: “A protest against” means an expression of objection to. Nothing in the text suggests that Sory or his sitters objected to the youth culture; the sitters were enthusiastic participants in it.

D.why_wrong: “A warning about” means an alert to some danger. The text gives no hint that the portraits caution anyone about the youth culture they show.

sources.what: Yossi Milo Gallery biography of Sanlé Sory: opened Volta Photo in Bobo-Dioulasso in 1960; supplied props such as Air Afrique flight bags, radios, telephones, lamps and record players; teenagers and 20-somethings playact as their favorite music icons while others model modern fashions; the portraits document exuberant youth culture in Burkina Faso following independence from France

items.notes: Subject: humanities (photography). Key letter B. A window into is not used (our own earlier key). Raw freq.txt ranks: departure 1,837; record 3,352; protest 2,749; warning 1,887.

items.subtype: Blank completion: cause or consequence clue
items.passage: The pirarucu, a fish of the Amazon basin, must regularly rise to the surface to breathe air. Because of this, experienced fishers can ______ the pirarucu living in a lake: Leandro Castello found that fishers’ counts of the fish as they surfaced closely matched population estimates from slower, more expensive mark-recapture studies.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Tally” means to count. Because pirarucu must come to the surface to breathe, fishers can see them and keep count, and the text says the fishers’ counts closely matched estimates from mark-recapture studies.

A.why_wrong: “Tame” means to make an animal gentle or obedient. The text is about counting the fish as they surface, not about training them.

B.why_wrong: “Breed” means to raise animals so that they produce young. The text describes fishers counting pirarucu in lakes, not raising them.

C.why_wrong: “Frighten” means to scare. Fishers count the fish by watching them surface; scaring them away would work against that, and nothing in the text suggests it.

sources.what: Castello 2004, A Method to Count Pirarucu Arapaima gigas: Fishers, Assessment, and Management, North American Journal of Fisheries Management 24: experienced fishers counted pirarucu at the moment of aerial breathing; counts were strongly correlated (r = 0.98) with mark-recapture abundance estimates, avoiding slow and expensive mark-recapture work

items.notes: Subject: natural science (fisheries ecology). Key letter D. Count was not used as the key because counting is an official option. Raw freq.txt ranks: tame 7,226; breed 7,595; frighten 5,613; tally 21,114.

items.passage: Tara Donovan builds her large-scale installations from ______ objects. Haze (2003), for example, is a wall made entirely of translucent plastic drinking straws, and other works are assembled from stacked plastic cups, standard pencils, paper plates, or Scotch tape.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Mass-produced” means made in large numbers in factories. The examples in the text, plastic drinking straws, plastic cups, standard pencils, paper plates, and Scotch tape, are all ordinary factory-made goods.

B.why_wrong: “Antique” means old and valuable. Plastic straws and cups, pencils, paper plates, and tape are everyday modern products, not antiques.

C.why_wrong: “Salvaged” means rescued from waste. The text lists the materials Donovan uses but says nothing about where she gets them or whether they had been thrown away.

D.why_wrong: “Imported” means brought in from another country. The text says nothing about where Donovan’s materials come from.

sources.what: Wikipedia, Tara Donovan: works made of everyday objects including toothpicks, standard pencils, plastic drinking straws, plastic and Styrofoam cups, paper plates and Scotch tape; Haze (2003) is composed entirely of translucent plastic drinking straws stacked against a wall

items.notes: Subject: humanities (sculpture). Key letter A. Everyday was not used as the key (our own earlier key); handcrafted is an existing option word. Raw freq.txt ranks: mass-produced unseen; antique 7,759; salvaged 28,551; imported 9,001.

items.passage: Bernard Rudofsky’s 1964 Museum of Modern Art exhibition Architecture Without Architects celebrated buildings designed without the help of ______. Its photographs showed houses, villages, and other structures from dozens of countries that had been shaped not by specialists but by the shared, ongoing work of whole communities.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Professionals” are people trained and paid for a particular kind of work, such as architects. The text says the buildings in the exhibition were shaped not by specialists but by whole communities, so they were designed without professional help.

A.why_wrong: “Residents” are the people who live in a place. The text says the buildings were shaped by whole communities, so they were made with residents’ help, not without it.

B.why_wrong: “Tourists” are visitors. The text says nothing about tourists; it contrasts specialists with the communities that shaped the buildings.

D.why_wrong: “Donors” are people who give money. The text says nothing about how the buildings were paid for.

sources.what: MoMA press release, November 11, 1964, Architecture Without Architects (Bernard Rudofsky): photographs of communal architecture in some 60 countries, produced not by specialists but by the spontaneous and continuing activity of a whole people

items.notes: Subject: humanities (architecture). Key letter C. Negation in without; the clue (not by specialists but by whole communities) follows in the next sentence. Raw freq.txt ranks: residents 12,732; tourists 10,347; professionals 3,565; donors 26,188.

items.passage: Nearly all spiders are predators that consume insects and other animals, but Bagheera kiplingi, a jumping spider of Mexico and Central America, is predominantly ______. Christopher Meehan and colleagues found that it feeds mainly on nutrient-rich leaf tips that certain acacia shrubs produce to nourish the ants inhabiting them.
items.stem: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
items.explanation: “Vegetarian” means eating plants rather than animals. The text contrasts Bagheera kiplingi with spiders that eat insects and other animals and says it feeds mainly on leaf tips produced by acacia shrubs.

A.why_wrong: “Social” means living in groups. The text is about what the spider eats, not whether it lives alone or with others.

C.why_wrong: “Carnivorous” means meat-eating. The word “but” sets Bagheera kiplingi apart from spiders that eat animals, and the text says it eats mainly plant tissue.

D.why_wrong: “Aquatic” means living in water. The text says the spider feeds on acacia shrubs; nothing suggests it lives in water.

sources.what: ScienceDaily 2009, First Spider Known To Science That Feeds Mainly On Plant Food: Bagheera kiplingi (Meehan, Olson and colleagues, Current Biology) feeds mainly on Beltian bodies, leaf tips that acacias produce to feed their resident ants, in Mexico and Costa Rica

items.notes: Subject: natural science (arachnology). Key letter B. Contrast clue (but) with the restatement in the next sentence, like 1.57 and 1.58. Raw freq.txt ranks: social 1,421; vegetarian 40,077; carnivorous 43,573; aquatic 29,185.
